entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible].) We are more then Conquerours] What is that? Triumphers, 2 Cor. 2.14. We doe over-overcome: becauſe through faith in Chriſt we overcome before we fight, and are ſecure of victory.

entries.title: Romans 8:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible], ſcil. Ex verbi praedicatione eſſicaci ut ind[ilegible]at tacitè hoc verbo. Beza.) For I am perſwaded] Or, I am ſure by what I have heard out of Gods Word. He that hath this full aſſurance of faith goes gallantly to heaven. What (ſaith the world) ſhould a rich man ail? The Iriſh ask ſuch, What they mean to die? But I wonder more at ſuch as have the riches of full aſſurance, yea, that have but the aſſurance of adherence, though not of evidence, what they mean to walk heavily. Mr Latimer ſaies, That the aſſurance of heaven is the ſweet-meats of the feaſt of a good conſcience: There are other dainty diſhes in this feaſt, but this is the banquet.

entries.title: Romans 8:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: From the love of God] viz. Wherewith he loved us. For he loveth his own to the end, and in the end, Joh. 13.1. See the Note there. (Joh. Manlij, loc. com.) The wife of Camerarius heard Sarcerius interpreting this text, and verſ. 35. thus, and was much comforted after a ſore conflict.

entries.title: Romans 9:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS any one is more aſſured of his own ſalvation, the more he deſireth the ſalvation of others. Charity is no churl; as we ſee herein Paul.

entries.title: Romans 9:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Continuall ſorrow] Such as a woman in travail hath. ([ilegible].) So Gal. 4 19.

entries.title: Romans 9:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Were accurſed,] Devoted to deſtruction, as thoſe malefactours among the Heathens were, that in time of common calamity were ſacrificed to their infernall gods, ([ilegible].) for pacifying their diſpleaſure, that the plague might ceaſe. Out of greateſt zeal to God, and love to his countrey-men, the Apoſtle wiſheth himſelf Anathema, that is, not to be ſeparated from the Spirit and grace of Chriſt (for ſo he ſhould have ſinned) but from the comforts of Chriſt, the happineſſe that comes in by Chriſt, as one well interpreteth it.

entries.title: Romans 9:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The adoption] For Iſrael was Gods firſt-born, and ſo higher then the Kings of the earth, Pſ. 89 27.

And the glory] The Ark of the Covenant, 1 Sam. 4.21. whence Judea is called the glorious land, Dan. 11.41.

The Covenants] The morall law in two tables.

The giving of the law] The judiciall law.

The ſervice] The ceremoniall law. ([ilegible])

The promiſes] Of the Goſpel made to Abraham, and his ſeed for ever. Theſe promiſes are a precious book, every lear whereof drops myrth and mercy.

entries.title: Romans 9:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of whom is Christ] This is as great an honour to all mankinde (how much more to the Jews?) as if the King ſh[ilegible]uld marry into ſome poor family of his Subjects.

entries.title: Romans 9:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not as though the word] That word of promiſe, v. 4. which is ſure-hold, Ye[ilegible] and Amen.

For they are not all Iſrael] Multi ſacerdotes & panci ſacer dotes, ſaith Chryſostom, multi in nominc, & panci in opere. So here.

entries.title: Romans 9:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Neither becauſe they are] This profiteth them no more then it did Dives, that Abraham called him Son.

entries.title: Romans 9:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The children of the promiſe] Abraham by beleeving Gods promiſe, begat, after a ſort, all beleevers, yea Chriſt himſelf, the head of his ſeed, his Son according to the fleſh, but more according to the faith.

entries.title: Romans 9:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: At this time] See the Note on Gen. 18.10.

entries.title: Romans 9:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But when Rebecca] She, and not Iſaac is named, becauſe ſhe received the Oracle; whether from the mouth of Melchiſedech, or ſome other way, I have not to determine.

entries.title: Romans 9:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For the children, &c.] Here the Apoſtle wadeth into that profundum ſine fundo, Predeſtination.

Being not yet born] Sapores ſon of Miſdates, King of Perſia, began his raign before his life. For his father dying left his mother with childe, and the Perſian Nobility ſet the Crown on his mothers belly, acknowledging thereby her iſſue for their Prince, before ſhe as yet had felt her ſelf quick. God elects not of fore-ſeen faith or works, but of free-grace.

entries.title: Romans 9:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall ſerve] Servitude came in with a curſe, and figureth reprobation, Gen. 9 25. Joh. 8 34 35. Gal. 4.30.

entries.title: Romans 9:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eſau have I hated] i. e. I have not loved him, but paſſed him by: and this praecerition is properly oppoſed to election.

entries.title: Romans 9:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is there] Carnall reaſon dares reprehend what it does not comprehend.

entries.title: Romans 9:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Bonavent. in lib. 1. ſent. diſt. 41. [ilegible] q. [ilegible].) I will have mercy, &c.] Dei voluntas eſt ratio rationum, nec tantùm recta, ſed regula.

entries.title: Romans 9:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So then it is not, &c.] Nec volentis, nec volantis (as a Noble-man gave it for his Motto) though a man could run as faſt as a bird can fire.

entries.title: Romans 9:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Raiſed thee up] For a veſſel of wrath, and an inſtance of my juſtice.

entries.title: Romans 9:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Therefore] God being a free agent, cannot be unjuſt: he is bound to none.

entries.title: Romans 9:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Why doth he yet finde fault?] Queritur, ſaith the Vulgar: which interpretation cozened Aquinas, as if it had been written Quaeritur. So Luk. 15.8. Gregory the great and others, for Everrit, reade Evertit: which miſtake produced many groundleſſe gloſ[ilegible]es.

entries.title: Romans 9:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That repliest against God] Gr. That chatteſt and wordest it with him? ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Romans 9:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of the ſame lump] The Apoſtle alludeth to mans creation, and therehence aſcendeth to Gods eternall decree of predeſtination.

entries.title: Romans 9:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Fitted to deſtruction] Non dicit Deum eos aptaſſe ad interitum, ne videretur dicere Deum eis indidiſſe peccatum, quo ad exitium praeparentur. (Molinaeus in Anat. Armin.)

entries.title: Romans 9:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And that he might] He rejected ſome, that his mercy might the more appear in the election of others.

entries.title: Romans 9:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Even us] Not me Paul only hath he aſſured of vocation, and ſo conſequently of election to eternall life.

entries.title: Romans 9:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And her beloved] Jer. 12.7. God cals the Church, the beloved of his ſoul, or (as the Septuagint and Vulgar reade it) his beloved ſoul. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Romans 9:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The children, &c.] This is ſuch a royalty, John 1.12. as the Apoſtle worthily wondereth at, and ſets an Ecce upon it.

entries.title: Romans 9:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Aremnant] Reſerved for royall uſe. Diaconos, paucitas honorabiles fecit, ſaith Hierom: Sic & ſanctos, ſay I.

entries.title: Romans 9:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A ſhort work] When once he ſets to work to cut off hypocrites.

entries.title: Romans 9:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Except the Lord of Sabaoth] That is, Of Hoſts. God is Commander in chief of all creatures. The Rabbins well obſerve that he hath Magnleh Cheloth, and Matteh Cheloth, (Kim[ilegible]b[ilegible],) two generall troops, as his horſe and foot, the upper and lower troops ready preſt.

entries.title: Romans 9:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which is of faith] Faith wraps it ſelf in the righteouſnes of Chriſt, and ſo juſtifieth us.

entries.title: Romans 9:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The law of righteouſnes] That is, The righteouſnes of the law.

entries.title: Romans 9:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For they ſtumbled] So they doe to this day. (Jo. Fox Chriſt. Triumphans [ilegible]piſt.) So do Papiſts and carnall Proteſtants. Non fruſtrà Lutherus in libris totiès vaticinatus videtur, ſeſe vereri dictitans, ne ſe extincto verailla juſtificationis diſciplina prorſus apud Chriſtianos exoleſcat.

entries.title: Romans 9:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on 1 Pet. 2.6.

entries.title: Romans 10:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SO it ſhould be ours. See my True Treaſure, Chapter 7. Sect. 2.

entries.title: Romans 10:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They have a zeal of God] So had thoſe two Rabbins, David Rubenita, (Alſted. Chron. 426.) and Shelomoh Molchu that ſet upon the Emperour Charles the fift, to perſwade him to Judaiſme, and were therefore put to a cruell death, anno 1530. So had Latimer before his converſion: I was as obſtinate a Papiſt, ſaith he, as any was in England: Inſomuch that when I ſhould be made Bachelour in Divinity, my whole Oration went againſt Philip Melancthon, and his opinions, &c. Being a Prieſt, and uſing to ſay Maſſe, he thought he had never ſufficiently mingled his maſſing wine with water: and moreover that he ſhould never be damned, if he were once a profeſſed Frier; (Act. and Mon. fol 1571.) with divers ſuch ſuperſtitious phantaſies. Zeal without knowledge is as wilde-fire in a fools hand; it is like the devil in the demoniack, that caſts him ſometimes into the fire, and ſometimes into the water.

entries.title: Romans 10:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For they being ignorant] The ſoul that is without knowledge is not good, and he that (without knowledge) hasteth with his feet, ſinneth, Prov. 19.2. the faſter he goeth, the farther he is out.

entries.title: Romans 10:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For Christ is the end, &c.] q. d. By, and for Chriſts ſake, is the righteouſnes of God. But the Jews ſubmit not to Chriſt, therefore not to the righteouſnes of God.

entries.title: Romans 10:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall live by them] This doe and live; that is, ſaith Luther, morere, die out of hand: for there is no man lives and ſins not. We can as little ceaſe to ſin, as the pulſe to beat, heart to pant, &c.

entries.title: Romans 10:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Say not in thine heart] The law preacheth faith in Chriſt, as well as the Goſpel.

entries.title: Romans 10:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Into the deep] Thoſe deeps of the earth, Pſ. 71.20.

entries.title: Romans 10:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The word is nigh thee] Moſes meant it of the law, but it more fitly agreeth to the Goſpel. The Babe of Bethlehem is ſwathed up in the bands of both Teſtaments: he is authour, object, matter and mark of both. Therefore if we will profit in hearing, teaching, reading, we muſt have the eye of our mindes turned toward Chriſt, as the faces of the Cherubims were toward the Mercy-ſeat.

entries.title: Romans 10:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That if thou ſhalt confeſſe] That is, If thou ſhalt call upon the name of the Lord, as it is expounded, v. 13.

entries.title: Romans 10:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For with the heart, &c.] Pluturch tels us, that of all plants in Aegypt, (Plut. de [ilegible]ſide & Oſiride.) that they call Perſica is conſecrated to their goddeſſe Iſis, and that for this reaſon, becauſe the fruit of it is like an heart, the leaf like a tongue.

entries.title: Romans 10:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall not be aſhamed] Maketh not haſte, ſaith the Prophet. Shame and confuſion follow haſte and procipitancy: Sed Deo confiſi nunquam confuſi.

entries.title: Romans 10:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is rich unto all, &c.] He cannot therefore be poor that can pray: for he ſhall have out his praier, either in money or moneys-worth.

entries.title: Romans 10:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall be ſaved] Though he miſſe of that particular mercy he asketh, he is certainly ſealed up to ſalvation.

entries.title: Romans 10:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How ſhall they hear, &c.] The word read, is of divine uſe and efficacy: but of preaching we may ſay as David did of Goliah's ſword, There's none to that.

entries.title: Romans 10:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How beautifull are the jeet] How much more their faces? Surely I have ſeen thy face as the face of God, ſaid Jacob to Eſau, Gen. 33.10. that is, honourable and comfortable. We know how Cornelius received Peter; and the Galatians, Paul, till they were bewitched from him, Gal. 4.14. But it muſt be remembred that we glorifie the Word, not the Preacher, Act. 13.48.

entries.title: Romans 10:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who hath beleeved our report!] Gr. Our hearing. ([ilegible]) Paſſively taken. So Caeſar and Cicero uſe auditio, for report and rumour. Some ſit before a preacher as ſenſleſſe as the ſeats they ſit on, pillars they lean to, dead bodies they tread on. Others rage, Tange montes & fumig abunt, &c.

entries.title: Romans 10:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By the word of God] That is, By the Word of Gods command ſending out preachers gifted for the purpoſe, and ſaying to them, Goe. preach, &c.

entries.title: Romans 10:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yes verily; their ſound, &c.] Sonus, tonus. David ſaith only, Their line, Pſal. 19.2. ([ilegible].) That accurate and artificiall frame of the heaven preacheth, as it were, the infinite wiſdome and power of the Creatour. All Gods works are his Regij profeſſores, his Catholike Preachers, or reall Poſtilles (as one calleth them) of his Divinity. The world (ſaith Clem. Alex.) is Dei Scriptura, Gods great Bible with three great leaves, heaven, earth and hell.

entries.title: Romans 10:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Did not Iſrael know] ſc. That the Gentiles were to be called? They were oft told it.

entries.title: Romans 10:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is very bold] So that for his boldnes he was ſawn aſunder, ſaith Hierom.

entries.title: Romans 10:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Stretched] A metaphor from a mother.

entries.title: Romans 11:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS I may ſeem to have ſaid, Chap. 10. Miniſters muſt doe their utmoſt to prevent miſtakes. Zuinglius, when in his Sermons he had terrified the wicked, was wont to ſhut up with Bone vi[ilegible], hoc nihil ad te, Thou good man, I mean not thee.

entries.title: Romans 11:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Saith of Elias] A man of ſuch tranſcendent zeal, that to heighten the expreſſion thereof, ſome have legended of him, that when he drew his mothers breſts, he was ſeen to ſuck in fire.

entries.title: Romans 11:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And I am left alone] To withſtand and reform the common corruptions. Some have commended it to our conſideration, that from the firſt ſervice in the Temple, when it was built, and the time of Eliah's Reformation, was about an hundred years: And from the Reformation in K. Edward the ſixth's daies untill now, is about the ſame proportion of time.

entries.title: Romans 11:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The image of Baal] [ilegible], to that Lady, as our modern Idolaters alſo call the virgin Mary, whom they deſpite with ſeeming honours. (Sal[ilegible]zar. Ieſuita in Prov. 8.19. Ibid ad ver. 23. Ibid. ad ver. 29.) They would perſwade the world, that Chriſt by dying obeyed not his Father only, but his mother too, that ſhe is the complement of the Trinity, that ſhe intreateth not, but commandeth her Sonne, is the moſt imperious Mother of our Judge, with many like horrid blaſphemies, which I tremble to relate.

entries.title: Romans 11:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: According to the election of grace] St Paul was Constantiſſimus gratiae praedicator, as Auſtin calleth him, a moſt conſtant preacher of Gods free grace.

entries.title: Romans 11:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Then is it no more of works] Whatſoever conferrumination of grace and works Papiſts dream of. They think, that as he that ſtandeth on two firm branches of a tree, is ſurer then he that ſtandeth upon one only: So he that truſteth to Chriſt and works too, is in the ſafeſt condition. But, 1. They are fallen from Chriſt that truſt to works, Gal. 5.4. 2. He that hath one foot on a firm branch, and another on a rotten one, ſtands not ſo ſure as if he ſtood wholly on that which is ſound. But let them be Moſes's Diſciples, let us be Chriſts: Set not up a candle to this Sun of righteouſneſſe: mix not thy puddle with his purple bloud, thy rags with his raiment, thy Pigeons plumes with his Eagles-feathers. He can and will ſave his to the utmoſt, Heb. 7.25. Deteſt all mock-ſtaies.

entries.title: Romans 11:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Iſrael] i. e. The carnall Iſraelite.

He ſeeketh for] viz. Righteouſnes and ſalvation by works.

Hardened] By a judiciary hardnes.

entries.title: Romans 11:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Spirit of ſlumber] So that with thoſe Bears in Pliny they cannot be awakened with the ſharpeſt prickles: and with thoſe Aſſes in Hetruria, that feeding upon hen-bane, (Mathiol in Dioſcorid.) they he for dead, and awake not till half-hileded. Such a dead Lethargy is now befallen Papiſts.

entries.title: Romans 11:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Be made a ſnare] As the bait is to the birds.

entries.title: Romans 11:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bow down] i. e. Bring them into bondage and miſery. Compare Lev. 26.13.

entries.title: Romans 11:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Have they ſtumbled] He that ſtumbleth and comes not down, gets ground.

entries.title: Romans 11:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How much more their fulneſſe] O dieculam illam! dexter mihi prae laetitia ſalit oculus. How long, Lord, holy and true?

entries.title: Romans 11:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I magnifie mine office] I make the utmoſt of it by gaining ſouls to Chriſt.

entries.title: Romans 11:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And might ſave ſome] Miniſters muſt turn themſelves as it were into all ſhapes and faſhions both of ſpirit and ſpeech to win people to God.

entries.title: Romans 11:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Be the reconciling] Not as a cauſe, but as an occaſion.

Life from the dead] That is, Res ſummè bona, ſaith Phocius, a ſpeciall good thing.

entries.title: Romans 11:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If the first fruit be holy] Not with a naturall, but federall holines, as 1 Cor. 7.14.

entries.title: Romans 11:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wert graffed in] Gr. ([ilegible].) Pricked into the middle, the center of the Olive.

entries.title: Romans 11:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Boast not] Gr. Throw not up thy neck, in a ſcornfull inſulting way, but rather pity and pray for them.

entries.title: Romans 11:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Iſidor. ſo[ilegible]il. Greg Moral.) Thou wilt ſay] Carnall reaſon will have ever ſomewhat to ſay, and is not eaſily ſet down.

entries.title: Romans 11:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Be not high-minded, but fear] Alterius perditio tua ſit cautio, ſaith one. Ruina majorum ſit cantela minorum, ſaith another, Seeſt thou thy brother ſhipwrackt? look well to thy tackling.

entries.title: Romans 11:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Take heed leſt] Cavebis autèm ſi pavehis.

entries.title: Romans 11:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible].) Severity] Gr. Reſection or cutting off, as a Chyrurgian cutteth off proud and dead fleſh.

entries.title: Romans 11:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God is able] He can fetch heart of oak out of an hollow tree, and of carnall make a people created again, Pſal. 102.18. Eph. 2.10.

entries.title: Romans 11:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Contrary] Therefore nature contributes nothing toward the work of converſion.

entries.title: Romans 11:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That blindeneſſe in part] It is neither totall nor perpetuall. Lyra was a famous Engliſh Jew. Tremellius was alſo a Jew born; they are but Methe mispar, a very few that are yet converted. (Spec. Europ.) They pretend (but maliciouſly) that thoſe few that turn Chriſtians in [ilegible]taly, are none other then poor Chriſtians hired from other cities to perſonate their part. But when God ſhall have united thoſe two ſticks, Ezek. 37.19. and made way for thoſe Kings of the Eaſt, Rev. 16.12. then it ſhall be ſaid of Jacob and Iſrael, What hath God wrought! Numb. 23.23.

entries.title: Romans 11:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall turn away ungodlineſſe] That is, He ſhall pardon their ſin. The Prophet Iſaiah hath it, Ʋnto them that turn from tranſgreſſion in Jacob, &c. They whoſe perſons are juſtified, have their luſts mortified.

entries.title: Romans 11:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When I ſhall take] By the ſpirit of judgement and of burning, Iſa. 4.4. with 27.9.

entries.title: Romans 11:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They are enemies] i. e. Hated of God, as appears by the oppoſition; and baniſhed, as it were, by a common conſent of Nations, out of humane ſociety. See 1 Theſſ. 2.15, 16.

entries.title: Romans 11:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Are without repentance] When God is ſaid to repent, it is Mutatiorei non Dei, effectus non affectus, facti non conſilij, a change not of his will, but of his work. Repentance with man, is the change of his will: Repentance with God, is the willing of a change.

entries.title: Romans 11:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Through their] By occaſion of their unbelief. Pungit Judaeos & humiliat Gentes, ſaith one.

entries.title: Romans 11:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That they alſo] It noteth not the cauſe, but the event, as 1 Cor. 11.19.

entries.title: Romans 11:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
([ilegible].) For God hath concluded] Or lockt them all up in the laws dark dungeon, Gal. 3.22. Unbelief breaks all the law at an inſtant by rejecting Chriſt, as the firſt act of faith obeys all the law at an inſtant in Chriſt.

That he might have mercy upon all] Luther in a very great conflict was relieved and comforted by the often repeating of this ſweet ſentence.

entries.title: Romans 11:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: O the depth of the riches] The Romans dedicated a certain lake, the depth whereof they knew not, to victory, ſo ſhould we the unſearchable counſels of God, being ſubdued to that, which we cannot ſubdue to our underſtandings.

entries.title: Romans 11:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who hath been his Counſellour] Alphonſo the wiſe (the fool rather) was heard blaſphemouſly to ſay, (Roderic, Santij Hiſt. Hiſpan. p. 4, [ilegible]. 5.) That if he had been of Gods counſell at the Creation, he could have adviſed and ordered many things much better then they now are.

entries.title: Romans 11:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who hath firſt given to him] Doe we not owe him all that we have and are? And can a man merit by paying his debts?

entries.title: Romans 11:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For of him] As the efficient cauſe, and (through him) as the adminiſtring cauſe, and (to him) as the finall cauſe are all things. A wiſe Philoſopher could ſay, That man is the end of all in a ſemicircle; that is, All things in the world are made for him, and he is made for God.

To whom be glory for ever] God (ſaith one) counts the works and fruits that come from us to be ours: becauſe the judgement and reſolution of will, whereby we do them is ours: This he doth to encourage us. But becauſe the grace whereby we judge and will aright, comes from God, aſcribe we all to him: So ſhall he looſe no praiſe, we no encouragement.

entries.title: Romans 12:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
AS they of old did their ſacrifices at the altar. With the burnt offering, wch ſignified the ſacrificing of the fleſh, was joyned the ſin-offering, that is, Chriſt, Faith applies Chriſt to the believer, & the believer to Chriſt.

Your bodies] That is, your whole perſon. Cainiſtae ſunt, ſaith Luther, offerentes non perſonam, ſed opus perſonae. They are Cainists that offer to God the work done, but do not offer themſelves to God.

A living ſacrifice] In the old law they had many kindes of Sacrifices killed and offered. Now (ſaith Origen) in ſtead of a Ramme we kill our irefull paſſions: in ſtead of a Goat our unclean affections: in ſtead of ſlying fowls our idle thoughts, &c.

entries.title: Romans 12:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
To this world] To the corrupt cuſtomes and courſes of wicked wordlings. See them ſet forth, Rom 13.13. Epheſ. 4.18, 19, 20. 1 Pet. 4.3. and ſhun them.

But be ye transformed] Gr. Metamorphoſed, the old frame being diflolved, and a new form acquited.

That ye may prove] ſc. By your practice.

entries.title: Romans 12:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible]. Xenoph. de dictu & factis Socrat. lib 3.) But to think ſoberly] Gr. To be wiſe to ſobriety. Socrates made no diſtinction between wiſdome and ſobriety, [ilegible] non diſtinguebat.

entries.title: Romans 12:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For as we have, &c.] See 1 Cor. 12.12, which is a Commentary on this text.

entries.title: Romans 12:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: One body in Chriſt] See the Note on 1 Cor. 12.12, 13.

entries.title: Romans 12:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: According to the proportion] That form of ſound words, 2 Tim. 1.13. thoſe principles of the doctrine of Chriſt, Heb. 6.1. with which all interpretations of Scripture muſt bear due proportion.

entries.title: Romans 12:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or Miniſtery] Take it either largely for the whole miniſtery, as 1 Cor. 12.5, Act. 1.17. Or more ſtrictly for the office of a Deacon, as Act. 6.

entries.title: Romans 12:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or he that exhorteth] The Paſtour properly ſo called. See the Note on Eph. 4.11.

entries.title: Romans 12:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible].) Abhorre that which is evil] Hate it as hell it ſelf: ſo the word ſignifies, Mihi certè Auxentius nunquam aliud quam [ilegible]abolus erit, quia Arrianus, ſaith Hilary, I ſhall look upon Auxemius no otherwiſe then as upon a devil, ſo long as he is an Arrian.

entries.title: Romans 12:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Be kindely affectioned] As naturall brethren and more. Arctior eſt copula cordis quam corporis. We are brethren in Adam according to the fleſh, in and by Chriſt according to the Spirit.

entries.title: Romans 12:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
([ilegible]. Cunctator.) Not ſlothfull] Or, Not driving off till it be too late. Charles the ſon of Charles Duke of Aniou, who was King of Sicily and Jeruſalem, was called, Carolus cunctator, not in the ſenſe as Fabius, becauſe he ſtaid till opportunity came, but becauſe he ſtaid till opportunity was loſt.

Fervent in ſpirit] Gr. Seething hot. God, ([ilegible].) who is himſelf a pure act, loveth activenes in men: the very reſt of heavenly bodies is in motion in their proper places.

entries.title: Romans 12:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Rejoycing in hope] Hope makes abſent joyes preſent, wants plenitudes, and beguiles calamity as good company doth the time.

Patient in tribulation] Bearing up under preſſures, as among many other Martyrs Nicolas Burton, who by the way to the ſtake, and in the ſ[ilegible]ame was ſo patient and chearfull, (Act. and Mon. 1866.) that the tormentours ſaid, the devil had his ſoul before he came to the fire, and therefore his ſenſes of feeling were paſt.

Continuing instant in praier] Conſtant and inſtant. ([ilegible]. N[ilegible]z. in Epita.) A metaphor from hunting dogs, that give not over the game till they have got it. Nazianzen ſaith of his ſiſter Gorgonia, that ſhe was ſo given to praier, that her knees ſeemed to grow to the very ground. Of Traſilla it is reported, (Greg. Dialog.) that being dead ſhe was found to have her elbows as hard as horn, by leaning to a desk at which ſhe uſed to pray. St James is ſaid to have had knees as hard as Camels knees, (Euſeb.) by his continuall kneeling in praier. And Paul the eremite was ſound dead kneeling upon his knees, holding up his hāds, lifting up his eye: ſo that the very dead corps ſeemed yet to live, and to pray to God. (Hieron in vita)

entries.title: Romans 12:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To the neceſſity] Gr. To the uſes of the Saints, ([ilegible].) not ſtaying till they be in neceſſity.

entries.title: Romans 12:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bleſſe them] See the Note on Mat. 5 44.

entries.title: Romans 12:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Weep with them that weep] St Cyprians compaſſion is remarkable, Cum ſingulis pectus meum copulo, maeroris & funeris pondera luctuoſa participo: cum plangentibus plango, cum d ſlentibus defleo, &c. I partake in every mans grief, and am as much affected and afflicted, as if it were mine own caſe.

entries.title: Romans 12:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Be of the ſame] This verſe had been eaſie, had not Interpreters obſcured it, as Origen obſerveth.

entries.title: Romans 12:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Recompenſe to no man] In reaſon, revenge is but juſtice: Aristotle commends it: the world cals it Manhood, (Ariſt Rhetor. lib. 9 cap. 1.) 'tis doghood rather. The manlier any man is, the milder and more mercifull, as David, 2 Sam. 1.12. and Julius Caeſar, who wept over Pompeys head preſented to him, and ſaid, Non mihi placet vindicta, dicta, ſed victoria, I ſeek not revenge, but victory.

entries.title: Romans 12:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As much as lieth in you] Let it not ſtick on your part. [ilegible]ive not offence careleſly, take not offence cauſleſly. See the Note on Mat. 5.9

entries.title: Romans 12:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Avenge not your ſelves] Some take the Sword into their own hands: and, leſt they ſhould ſeem Anabaptiſts in taking two blows for one, will give two blows for one.

Give place to wrath] ſc. To the wrath and vengeance of God, which he ſeemeth to prevent that ſeeks revenge.

entries.title: Romans 12:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt heap] Thou ſhalt melt him, and make him thy friend for ever.

entries.title: Romans 12:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Be not overcome] In rixa is inferior eſt, qui victor eſt, ſaith Baſil. In revenge of injuries, he is the loſer that gets the better. ([ilegible] [ilegible]. [ilegible] Cor. 6.7.) Hence the Apoſtle diſgraceth it, by a word that ſignifieth diſgrace or loſſe of victory.

But overcome evil] This is the moſt noble victory. Thus David overcame Saul, (Func. Chronol.) and Henry the 7th, Emperour of Germany, overcame the Prieſt that poiſoned him at the Sacrament: for he pardoned him, and bad him be packing. So did not Iacup the Perſian King, (Turk Hiſt.) who perceiving himſelf poiſoned by his adulterous wife, enforced her to drink of the ſame cup: and becauſe he would be ſure ſhe ſhould not eſcape, with his own hand he ſtruck off her head. But this (to ſay truth) was not revenge, but juſtice.

entries.title: Romans 13:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
IN things lawfull only: for elſe we muſt anſwer as thoſe Apoſtles did, Act. 3.29. and as Polycarp, who being commanded to blaſpheme Chriſt, and to ſwear by the fortune of Caeſar, peremptorily refuſed, and ſaid, We are taught to give honour to Princes and Potentates, but ſuch honour as is not contrary to Gods religion.

Ordained of God] In regard of it's inſtitution, (Tha. 2.2. q. 10. ar. 10.) though for the manner of it's conſtitution it is of man.

entries.title: Romans 13:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Reſisteth the power] His authorative commands, not his perſonall.

Receive to themſelves damnation] Poenam ſibi auferent, ſaith Piſcator, ([ilegible]. Conſer. 1 Cor. 11.31, 32) they ſhall receive puniſhment, to wit from the Magiſtrate: as Aretine deſerved to doe, who by longer cuſtome of libellous and contumelious ſpeaking againſt Princes, had got ſuch a habit, that at laſt he came to diminiſh and diſeſteem God himſelf.

entries.title: Romans 13:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For Rulers are not, &c.] They ſhould not be. But Ieroboam ſet a net on Mizpeh, and ſpread a ſhare upon Tabor to watch who would go from him to Iudah to worſhip, Hoſ 5.1.

A terrour to good works, but to the evil] The Sword of juſtice (ſaith one) muſt be furbiſhed with the oil of mercy: yet there are caſes wherein ſeverity ought to caſt the ſcale. (Petr. Nicol. Gelſtrou[ilegible]. Dan. biſt.) Dureſce, Dureſce, ò infoelix Lantgravie, ſaid the poor Smith to the Lantgrave of Thuring, more milde then was for his peoples good. Bonis nocet, qui malis parcit. Edward the Confeſſour was held a bad Prince, not by doing, but enduring ill.

entries.title: Romans 13:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For he is the minister] It was written upon the ſword of Charles the great, Decem praeceptorum custos Carolus, Charles is Lord Keeper of the Decalogue.

For he beareth not the Sword in vain] Like St Paul in a glaſſe window, or St George (as they call him) in a ſign-poſt.

A revenger to execute wrath] But now we ſee how every man almoſt will be a Pope in his own cauſe, depoſe the Magiſtrate, at leaſt appeal from him to himſelf.

entries.title: Romans 13:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But alſo for conſcience ſake] Good Rulers we muſt obey as God, bad, for God. ([ilegible]. Baſil.)

entries.title: Romans 13:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Attending continually] As born for the benefit of many. The Parliament in the 25. of Edward 3. is known to poſterity by the name of Benedictum Parliamentum: So ſhall this preſent [ilegible]arliament for their continuall attendance upon the Lords work; bending themſelves to the buſineſſe (as the word ſignifies) and holding cut therein with unparallel'd patience. (This was written, anno 1646. [ilegible].)

entries.title: Romans 13:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Render therefore to all their dues] He ſaith not their unjuſt exactions. Melancthon makes mention of a cruell Prince, that to get money of his Subjects, would knock out their teeth; (Primò unum dentem evellebat minitans, &c.) firſt one tooth, and then another, unleſſe they would bring him in ſuch ſums of money as he required.

Fear to whom, &c.] i. e. Reverentiall obſervance, farre beyond that which Q. Fabius Maximus yeelded to his ſon, when he became Conſul. (Li. Decal. 3. lib 4.)

entries.title: Romans 13:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Owe no man, &c.] The Perſians reckoned theſe two for very great ſins; 1. To be in debt. 2. To tell a lie; the later being oft the fruit of the former. By the twelve Tables of Rome, (Xenophon.) he that owed much, and could not pay, was to be cut in pieces, and every creditour was to have a piece of him according to the debt. (Gell lib. 12. c. 1.)

entries.title: Romans 13:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible].) Briefly comprehended] Capitulated, fulfilled, ſaith the Syriack, ſummed up. St Bartholomew was quoted by Dionyſius to have ſaid of Divinity, Et magnam eſſe & minimam, that it was large and yet little, ([ilegible].) as containing much matter in few words.

entries.title: Romans 13:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The [ilegible] of the law] The filling up of the law in this, that it clotheth the duties of the law with the glory of a due manner, and ſeateth them upon their due ſubjects, with the unwearied labours of a conſtant well-doing.

entries.title: Romans 13:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
To awake out of ſleep] Whiles the Crocodile ſleepeth with open mouth, the Indian rat gets into his ſtomack, and eateth thorow his entrails. Whiles Iſhhoſheth ſlept upon his bed at noon, Baanah and Rechab took a way his head. Security uſhereth in deſtruction. Goe forth and ſhake your ſelves as Sampſon did, when the Philistims were upon him: leſt Satan ſerve you, at leaſt for your ſouls, as Captain Drake did the Spaniard at Taurapaſa in the Weſt-Indies for his treaſure; he found him ſleeping ſecurely on the ſhore, and by him thirteen bars of ſilver to the value of 400000 duckets, (Co[ilegible]dens Eliſa. fol. 422.) which he commanded to be carried away, not ſo much as once waking the man. Or leſt Chriſt himſelf deal by us, as Epaminondas did by the watchman, whom he found aſleep: He thruſt him thorow with his ſword, and being blamed for ſo ſevere a fact, he replied, Talem eum reliqui, qualem inveni, I left him, as I found him.

For now is our ſalvation nearer] Stir up your ſelves therefore, and ſtrain toward the mark. ([ilegible]. Heſych. Poliux l 3 [ilegible] 30) There is a Greek word ſignifying the end of a race, which is derived of a word that ſignifieth to ſpur or prick forward. Surely, as they that run their horſes for a wager, ſpur hardeſt at the races end: ſo, ſith our ſalvation is nearer now then ever it was, therefore we ſhould run faſter now then ever we did.

entries.title: Romans 13:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The night] Here it is taken for all unregeneracy, which (as the night) is full of errour, terrour. &c. Nox pudore vacat. This night with the Saints is far ſpent, or already paſt, as Cyprian and Hierom here render it. (Tranſivit. Praeterijt. [ilegible])

entries.title: Romans 13:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Let us walk honeſtly] Handſomely, faſhionably, mannerly, with an holy ſhamefacednes.

Not in chambering] Properly, lying a bed, or long-lying. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Romans 13:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
But put ye on] Augustin confeſſeth that he was converted by reading and pondering this text.

And make not proviſion] Make not projects, cater not for the fleſh.

entries.title: Romans 14:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
THat is not thorowly perſwaded of all things pertaining to Chriſtian liberty about things indifferent.

Receive] Aſſectu charitatis, put him into your boſoms, (Haymo.) bear with his weakneſſes, &c, Bucer rejected none, though different in ſome opinions, in whom he found, Aliquid Chriſti, any thing of Chriſt, whoſe weaklings are to be handled with all tenderneſſe.

But not to doubtfull] Make him not Queſtion-ſick, 1 Tim. 6.4. Wring not mens conſciences, you may hap to break the wards, if you do.

entries.title: Romans 14:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eateth herbs] Rather then meats forbidden by the Law. The ancient Latines were as well apaid of herbs to eat, (Dan. 1, 11.) as if they had had all manner of dainties. (Holus [ilegible].) Green herbs were both food and phyſick to them.

entries.title: Romans 14:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For God hath received him] viz. For his houſhold ſervant, which David counted a greater dignity then to be King of Iſrael. And Iuſtinian the Emperour ſtiled himſelf, Ʋltimum ſervorum Dei, the meaneſt of Gods ſervants.

entries.title: Romans 14:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who art thou, &c.] The wiſdome from above is without cenſuring, without hypocriſie, ſaith S. Iames, Chap. 3.17. Intimating, that the greateſt cenſurers are moſtly the greateſt hypocrites: And as any one is more wiſe, he is more ſparing of his cenſures.

entries.title: Romans 14:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let every man be fully perſwaded] It is a ſafe rule, (Plin. Epiſt:) Quod dubites, ne feceris: In doubtfull caſes be ſure to take the ſuter ſide.

entries.title: Romans 14:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For he giveth God thanks] A cuſtome uſed by the very Heathens to their gods, (Sir Ed Sands, Spec. Europae.) as is to be read in Homer and Virgil: but grown clean out of uſe among the Catholikes in France and Italy. But if they that give thanks at meat do eat to God, to whom do they eat that give none?

entries.title: Romans 14:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For none of us liveth to himſelf] S. Paul ſtood, as it were on tiptoes, ([ilegible].) Phil. 1.20 to ſee which way he might beſt glorifie God, by life or by death.

entries.title: Romans 14:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We are the Lords] Death divides us not from Chriſt, but brings us home to him, 2 Cor. 5.6. It is but winking (as that Martyr ſaid) and thou ſhalt be in heaven preſently.

entries.title: Romans 14:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That he might be Lord] He wonne his crown before he wore it: he fought for it, and having vanquiſhed all enemies, he accompliſhed and proclaimed the victory in his glorious reſurrection, triumphed in his wonderfull aſcenſion leading captivity captive, &c. Eph. 4.7.

entries.title: Romans 14:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But why doſt thou, &c.] Three things are not ſubject to our judgement. 1. The counſels of God. 2. The holy Scriptures. 3. The perſons of men. Be not therefore raſh in rejecting, or ſowr in cenſuring your fellow-ſervant; but let your moderation herein be known to all men; and the rather, becauſe the Lord is at hand, Phil. 4.5.

entries.title: Romans 14:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As I live, ſaith the Lord] As true as I live is an oath, as appears here, and Numb. 14 21. with Pſ. 95.11. Forbear it therefore.

entries.title: Romans 14:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So then every one, &c.] It was excellent counſell that the Oratour gave his hearers, (Cic. 4. in Verr.) I [ilegible]a vivamus ut ration[ilegible]m nobis reddendans arbitremur. Let us ſo live as thoſe that muſt give an account of all at laſt.

entries.title: Romans 14:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A ſtumbling block, or an, &c.] A lighter or greater offence, to make him go halting to heaven.

entries.title: Romans 14:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By the Lord Ieſus] Who hath pulled down the partition-wall, and purchaſed our Chriſtian liberty.

entries.title: Romans 14:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But if thy brother be grieved] It is his weakneſſe to be grieved thereat, but gratifie him howſoever. What one ſpeaks of a plain place of Scripture, this verſe (ſaith he) had been eaſie, had not Commentatours made it knotty: the like, ſaith another of a Chriſtians condition, it is gracious, happy, clear, ſure, ſweet, did not erroneous judgements vex and unſettle them.

entries.title: Romans 14:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Let not then your good] That is, Your Chriſtian liberty purchaſed by Chriſt.

Be evil spoken of] Gr. Be blaſphemed. Contumely caſt upon the people of God is blaſphemy in the ſecond Table. God, for the honour that he beareth to his people, counts and calls it ſo.

entries.title: Romans 14:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For the kingdome of God, &c.] That was a ſwiniſh ſaying of Epicurus, That eternall life ſhould be nothing elſe but a continuall eating of the fat, and drinking of the ſweet, ([ilegible].) even unto an unceſſant ſurfetting and drunkenneſſe. The Turks at this day promiſe Paradiſe to ſuch as die in warre for the Mahometan faith, (Blou[ilegible]ts voiage, p 37 [ilegible].) where they ſhall have delicious fare, pleaſant gardens, all ſenſuall delights, eternally to be enjoyed not withſtanding any former ſins. Fit lettice for ſuch lips.

entries.title: Romans 14:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is acceptable to God] And he is an happy man that can be acquitted by himſelf in private, in publike by others, in both by God.

entries.title: Romans 14:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wherewith one may edifie another] Diſcords among good people, do edificare in gehennam, as Tertullian phraſeth it, build backwards. One of the main ſcandals the Jews take from Proteſtants, is their diſſention.

entries.title: Romans 14:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The work of God] That work of faith, 1 Theſſ. 1.3. wrought by the mighty power of God, Epheſ. 1.19. who puts not forth great power, but for great purpoſes.

entries.title: Romans 14:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is good neither to eat, &c.] It will be no grief of heart (as ſhe once told David in another caſe) to have forborn in caſe of ſcandall. A great grief it would be if by ſome raſh word we ſhould betray a brother, or ſmite out the eie of our deareſt childe. (1 Sam. 25.) Should we then deſtroy the life of grace in another by our unadviſed walking?

entries.title: Romans 14:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Haſt thou faith?] Poſſe, & nolle, nobile eſt. Forbear for fear of effence, unleſſe it be in point of neceſſary duty: For then we may not doe evil that good may come, Rom. 3 8.

entries.title: Romans 14:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is damned] Both of his doubting conſcience, which ſoundeth heavily, as a ſhau[ilegible]m, and of God, who is greater then his conſcience.

entries.title: Romans 15:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
AS Porters do their burdens, as pillars do the poiſe of the houſe, ([ilegible].) or rather as parents bear their babes in their arms.

And not to pleaſe our ſelves] Bis deſipit, qui ſibi ſapit. Prov. 3.7.

entries.title: Romans 15:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pleaſe his neighbour] Though he croſſe himſelf: this is true Chriſtian love, and driven almoſt out of the world by ſinfull ſelf-love, which can eth men to diſlike thoſe things in others, that they ſlatter in themſelves.

entries.title: Romans 15:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For even Chriſt] And we ſhould expreſſe him to the world, preach abroad his vertues by our practice, 1 Pet. 2.9. Our lives ſhould be as ſo many Sermons upon the life of Chriſt. This is walk in Chriſt, Col. 2 6. as Chriſt, 1 Joh. 3.6.

entries.title: Romans 15:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For whatſoever things, &c.] Here the Apoſtle meets with an Objection. For ſome man might ſay, that that ſaying of the Pſalme pertains to David, how therefore is it applied to Chriſt? He anſwers, Whatſoever things, &c. q. d. We muſt learn to ſee Chriſt in David: David in the hiſtory, Chriſt in the myſtery; David as the type, Chriſt the truth.

That we through patience] Hence the Scriptures are called. (R[ilegible]vel. 2.) The word of Chriſts patience, becauſe they patient the heart under Gods holy hand: and are better called Phyſick for the ſoul, then ever was the library of Alexandria. ([ilegible].)

And comfort of the Scriptures] As the bloud and ſpirits are conveied by the veins and arteries: ſo is the Spirit by the promiſes, helping the ſoul to lay it ſelf upon Chriſt by faith, which is a grace of union, and ſo of eſtabliſhment.

entries.title: Romans 15:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Now the God of patience] The ſoul is then only in good plight, when the heaven anſwers the earth, Hoſ. 2.21. When. Chriſt the Sun of righteouſnes ſhines into it.

entries.title: Romans 15:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With one minde, and one mouth] It is recorded to the high commendation of the Church of Scotland, that for this 90 years and upwards, they have kept unity with purity, without ſchiſme, much leſſe hereſie. (Syntag. Confeſſion praeſat.)

entries.title: Romans 15:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To the glory of God] That is, Of heaven, the joyes whereof it is as impoſſible to comprehend, as it is to compaſſe the heaven with a ſpan, or contain the Ocean in a nut-ſhell. Such comfort there is in the preſence of Chriſt (though but in the womb) as it made John to ſpring: What then ſhall it be in heaven?

entries.title: Romans 15:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Now I ſay that Jeſus] Paul proveth particularly in this and the following verſes, that Chriſt hath taken both Jews and Gentiles to his glory.

entries.title: Romans 15:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And that the Gentiles] Though they had no ſuch promiſes, might glorifie Gods free grace in the day of their viſitation.

entries.title: Romans 15:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Rejoyce] That your names alſo are written in heaven, and that ye are enrolled in the records of the new Jeruſalem.

entries.title: Romans 15:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All ye Gentiles] As being received into the glory of God, verſ. 7.

entries.title: Romans 15:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In him ſhall the Gentiles truſt] I ſaith hath it, To him ſhall the Gentiles ſeek; To ſeek to God then argues truſt in God. He that hopes not, praies not, or but faintly.

entries.title: Romans 15:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Fill you with all joy, &c.] Note here that joy and peace are the means, whereby faith worketh hope.

entries.title: Romans 15:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Full of goodneſſe] The excellency of a godly man is to follow God fully, as Caleb, Numb. 14.24. to have a heart full of goodneſſe, as theſe Romans, a life full of good works, as Tabitha, Act. 9.36. Theſe ſhall receive a full reward, 2 Joh. 8.

entries.title: Romans 15:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Chryſoſtome truly ſaith of St Paul that he was inſatiabilis Dei cultor, one that thought he could never do God or his Church ſervice enough.

entries.title: Romans 15:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Miniſtring the Gospel] Serving about holy things, ([ilegible].) or doing ſacred offices, as the Prieſts under the Law, to whom the Apoſtle all along this verſe alludes in an elegant allegory: the Miniſtery is a divine and heavenly function. All other callings are for the world, and draw to the world: but this, both in the preparation and execution, draweth to God, keepeth us with God, and to be ever mindefull of the things of God.

entries.title: Romans 15:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I have therefore, &c.] So have all Gods faithfull Miniſters at this day againſt the contempts and contumelies caſt upon them by the mad world, ever beſides it ſelf in point of ſalvation. There is a pamphlet lately publiſhed that ſticks not to make that ſacred and tremend function of the Miniſtery to be as meer an impoſture, as very a myſtery of iniquity, (The Compaſſ. Samarit[ilegible]n.) as arrant a juggle as the Pa[ilegible]acy it ſelf.

entries.title: Romans 15:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To make the Gentiles, &c.] Chriſt by his Goſpel ſubdued the Britans, whom the Romans with all their force could never ſubdue, as Tertullian obſerved. (Britannorum [ilegible]nac[ilegible]ſſa Raman[ilegible] [ilegible] C[ilegible]riſto [ilegible] ſub[ilegible]ta 1 ere,)

entries.title: Romans 15:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So that from Jeruſalem] Chryſoſtome obſerveth, that Plato came three times to Sicily to convert Dionyſius the tyrant to morall philoſophy, and could not. But Paul fet a great compaſſe, converted many ſouls, planted many Churches: And why? Chriſt ſat upon him as upon one of his white horſes, and went forth conquering and to conquer, Revel 6.2.

entries.title: Romans 15:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Leſt I ſhould build[Leſt I ſhould ſeem to doe any thing unbeſeeming the office of an Apoſtle. There is a decorum to be kept in every calling.

entries.title: Romans 15:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But as it is written] In obedience to this divine oracle, the Apoſtle preached to thoſe that had not heard, yet neglected not thoſe that had.

entries.title: Romans 15:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For which cauſe] By planting Churches, and preaching where was more need.

entries.title: Romans 15:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Theſe many years] The Romans were converted to the faith betimes.

entries.title: Romans 15:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For I truſt to ſee you] Ipſe aſpectus viri beni delectat, ſaith Seneca. There is a great deal of ſweetneſſe in the ſociety of Saints, and much good to be gotten thereby. Sometimes, (ſaith a grave Divine) though we know that which we ask of others, as well as they doe, yet good ſpeeches will draw us to know it better, by giving occaſion to ſpeak more of it; wherewith the ſpirit works more effectually, and imprints it deeper, ſo that it ſhall be a more rooted knowledge then before. For that doth good that is graciouſly known, and that is graciouſly known, that the Spirit ſeals upon our ſouls.

entries.title: Romans 15:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To minister unto the Saints] The higheſt Angel in heaven may not hold himſelfe too good to ſerve the Saints.

entries.title: Romans 15:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ([ilegible].) It hath pleaſed them] It hath not been ſqueezed out of them, as verjuice is out of a crab, but freely and chearfully they have contributed.

entries.title: Romans 15:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Their debters they are] And ſo are we to pity and pray for them. See my True Treaſure, Sect. 2. chap.7.

entries.title: Romans 15:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
When I have ſealed] That is, Safely delivered, as if it were under ſeal.

This fruit] This ſweet ripe fruit of their faith and love, their alms

entries.title: Romans 15:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the fulneſſe of the bleſſing] Chriſt may uſe one of leſſe grace to doe more good then one of more (for there are diverſities of operations, as well as of gifts, 2 Cor. 12.6.) but uſually he delights to honour thoſe of moſt ſinicerity, with moſt ſucceſſe, 1 Cor. 15.10.

entries.title: Romans 15:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For the Lord Jeſus Christs ſake] This is one of thoſe paſſages in S. Paul, then the which there can nothing poſſibly be imagined more grave, divine, excellent, ſaith Beza.

That ye ſtrive together] Even to an agony, as the word imports. ([ilegible]) Spirituall beggery is the hardeſt and richeſt of all trades, as one laid. Learn of this great Apoſtle to beg praiers with all earneſtneſſe. (Act. and Mon. fol 1565. Ibid. 1499.) Pray for me, I ſay, pray for me, I ſay, quoth father Latymer, Pray for me, pray for me, for Gods ſake pray for me, ſaid bleſſed Bradford.

entries.title: Romans 15:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That my ſervice which, &c.] One would have thought that the Apoſtle coming with alms to them, ſhould eaſily have been well accepted: but he ſaw cauſe to ſeek God for ſuch a mercy, ſith it is he alone that faſhions mens opinions, and gives favour and kinde acceptance. Beſides wiſdome, he gave Solomon honour.

entries.title: Romans 15:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Be refreſhed] See the Note on Rom. 1.12. and on 2 Ioh. 12.

entries.title: Romans 15:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Now the God of peace] A ſit attribute for the preſent purpoſe. It is a commendable policy in Chriſtians, when they pray to propound God to their minde in ſuch notions, and under ſuch titles, as whereby they may ſee in God the things they deſire of God.

entries.title: Romans 16:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Diaconiſſe to miniſter to the ſick, as 1 Tim. 5.9. not a praedicantiſſe, to preach or have Peters keys at her girdle. (D. Baſtwick againſt Independ.)

entries.title: Romans 16:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As becometh Saints] Who are great Princes, States, in all lands, Pſal 4; and to be obſerved accordingly, even worthy of God, 3 Ioh. 6.

entries.title: Romans 16:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Salute Priſcilla] She is firſt mentioned, haply as more forward then her husband in the beſt things. So was Manoahs wife, and Nazianzens mother.

entries.title: Romans 16:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who have for my life] A rare example. (Dan. hiſt. 231.) Faſt friends are in this age for the moſt part gone on pilgrimage (ſaid one once) and their return is uncertain.

entries.title: Romans 16:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The Church that is in their houſe] The houſe of George Prince of Anhalt, for the good orders therein obſerved, is ſaid to have been, Eccleſia, Academia, Curia.

The first fruits of Achaia] The firſt that received the Goſpel there. A ſingular commendation, a ſweet happineſſe. Gods ſoul hath deſired ſuch firſt ripe fruits, Mic, 7.1. ſuch primroſes.

entries.title: Romans 16:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Greet Mary, &c.] It is profitable that men of great parts and place ſhould preſerve their memory with others, though it be but in a ſalutation: for it may be a means to fire up affection to godlineſſe in ſuch whom they ſo remember.

entries.title: Romans 16:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who are of note] Noble, notable Chriſtians, old experienced gray-headed Diſciples. ([ilegible].) Chriſtianity findes or makes us honourable.

entries.title: Romans 16:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Greet Amplias] Piety is no enemy to courteſie: It doth not remove, but rectifie it.

entries.title: Romans 16:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Our helper in Christ] A ſweet ſign to him, that his name was written in the book of life, Phil. 4.3.

entries.title: Romans 16:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Approved in Chriſt] An high ſtile, far beyond that of the great Turk, with all his big-ſwoln-titles.

entries.title: Romans 16:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: My kinſman] In the fleſh, but more in the faith, that ſureſt tie.

entries.title: Romans 16:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who labour in the Lord] Though not ſo much as Perſis did, (Cic. deorator.) yet doth he not defraud them of their due commendation, Prima ſequentem honestum eſt in ſecundis tertiiſque conſiſlere. Every man muſt not look to excell: let him be doing, as he is able.

entries.title: Romans 16:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His mother and mine] His by nature, mine by affection. The Apoſtles parted with parents and friends at home, found them abroad.

entries.title: Romans 16:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Salute Aſyncritus, &c.] Nothing is ſaid of theſe; for haſte perhaps, or elſe becauſe they were (as one ſaith of Ieſſe the father of David) Viri, probi & honeſti, minùs [ilegible]amen clari, Good honeſt men, but not much noted. Or laſtly, for that the Apoſtle had no very good opinion of them, as he ſeems not to have had of Demas, Coloſ. 4.14. who yet would needs be one in the Apoſtles regiſter there: a place he will have, though it be the laſt place. Hermas here mentioned, was reputed by ſome of the Ancients to be the Authour of that Apocryphall book called Paſtor; wherein he dealt not ſo fairly and faithfully in relating what he had received from the Apoſtles, being ſubleſtae fidci author.

entries.title: Romans 16:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Olympas] Viri nomen non mulicris. The name not of a woman, but of a man, ſaith Beza.

entries.title: Romans 16:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With an holy kiſſe] The Independents at Arnheim in Holland, (M. Edwards his Antapol. p 36, 60.) propounded this kiſſe of love to be practiſed amongſt them. So for anointing the ſick with oil, ſinging of hymns by one man, all the reſt being ſilent, &c.

entries.title: Romans 16:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
([ilegible].) Mark them which] Set a watchfull and a jealous eye upon them, as upon peſts and enemies. And here, let not our Epiſcopi (whoſe office it is chiefly) be Apoſcopi, (Bernard.) over-ſeers be by-ſeers, but look well to the ſlock, leſt theſe wolves worry them. (Act. 20, 29.)

And avoid them] Gr. Decline them ſtudiouſly, ([ilegible].) as ye would do a ſerpent in your way, or poiſon in your meats.

entries.title: Romans 16:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
But their own bellies] They pretend the ſervice of Chriſt to their worldly and wicked reſpects, by a diſſembled ſanctity, which is double iniquity. The Duke of Bavaria is even eaten up with thoſe Popiſh fleſh-ſhes, Friers and Jeſuites.

And by good words, &c.] Thoſe locuſts in the Revelation have faces like women, inſinuative and flattering. (Tertullian.) The Valentinian heretikes had an art to perſwade before they taught, whereas the truth perſwadeth by teaching, it doth not teach by perſwading.

They deceive] As cheaters do, by the cogging of a dye, Eph. 4.14. Fallax artiſicium, vel potiùs artiſex fallacia, ([ilegible]) ſaith Eraſmus on that text, a cunning kinde of cez[ilegible]nage.

entries.title: Romans 16:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For your obedience, &c.] Whereas the Romans might object, Are we alſo of thoſe ſimple ones? Your obedience, ſaith he, is famous all the world over. Howbeit I would have you wiſe to that which is good, but ſimple concerning evil. This ſimplicity is no diſparagement, to be unskilled in the devils depths, Revel. 2.24.

entries.title: Romans 16:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall bruiſe Satan] Sincerity of a little grace ſhall be rewarded with abundance of greater graces. Chriſt our Champion hath already wonne the field, and will ſhortly ſet our feet upon the necks of our ſpirituall enemies. The broken horns of Satan ſhall be the Trumpets of our triumph, and the Cornets of our joy.

entries.title: Romans 16:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Timotheus my work fellow] Of Timothy, reade Act, 16.1, 2. Of Lucius, Act. 13.1. Of Iaſon, Act. 17.5. Of Sopater, Act. 20 4.

entries.title: Romans 16:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I Tertius who wrote, &c.] Either from the Apoſtles mouths, or rather out of his foul papers.

entries.title: Romans 16:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gaius mine hoſt] Baptized by Paul, for whom therefore, (1 Cor. 1.14. Muli[ilegible] bo[ilegible]piti[ilegible] praebuit. Steph.) and for other good men he thought he could never doe enough. Such another was Phebe, verſe 2. who had been a ſuccourer, or an hoſteſſe to many, and to my ſelf, ſaith Paul.

entries.title: Romans 16:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The grace of our Lord] This is the ſeal of all S. Pauls Epiſtles. 2 Theſſ. 3.17.

entries.title: Romans 16:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which was kept ſecret] Even from the very Angels, 1 Pet. 1.12. who do daily profit in the knowledge of this ſecret, Eph. 3.10.

entries.title: Romans 16:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: According to the Commandment] The writings of the Prophets concerning the myſtery of Chriſt were not made known to the world by hap-hazard, but by a ſpeciall command of God.

entries.title: Romans 16:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To God only wiſe, &c.] So ſay I for theſe few Notes thus finiſhed.
